In leprosy patients, HLA-B*13:01 has been associated with development of this syndrome, an allele found at varying frequencies in Chinese, Japanese, Indian, and Southeast Asian populations but largely absent in Europeans and Africans. [Chapter: 31 Dermatitis Herpetiformis and Linear IgA Bullous Dermatosis, p.680]
chapter: 31 Dermatitis Herpetiformis and Linear IgA B­ullous Dermatosis

question: Among the topical antipsoriatic agents discussed, which one is contraindicated in pregnancy, and what teratogenic and embryotoxic effects have been observed with it in animal studies?
answer: Tazarotene is contraindicated in pregnancy (carries an embryo-fetal toxicity warning, former FDA category X). In animal studies it caused retinoid-type malformations such as spina bifida, hydrocephaly, and heart defects, as well as embryotoxic effects including reduced fetal body weight and skeletal ossification, although healthy deliveries have been reported with topical use. [Chapter: 8 Psoriasis, p.220-221]

question: Histologically, what feature distinguishes common warts and palmoplantar warts from flat warts in terms of surface architecture, and what characteristic vacuolated cell finding is unique to flat warts?
answer: Common warts and deep palmoplantar warts show marked papillomatosis (with palmoplantar warts having a cup-shaped invagination from inward-bowing lateral edges), whereas flat warts show no or only minimal papillomatosis, instead featuring orthokeratosis alternating with parakeratosis and a uniformly thickened granular layer. Flat warts are distinguished by vacuolization of cells in the granular and upper spinous layers, termed "bird's eyes." [Chapter: 79 Human Papillomaviruses, p.1699]

question: What is the human clinical phenotype associated with homozygous mutations in the gene encoding the integrin α3 subunit, and what basement membrane defect is seen in mice with targeted deletion of this subunit?
answer: In humans, homozygous mutations in the gene encoding the integrin α3 subunit cause basement membrane disruption resulting in congenital nephrotic syndrome, interstitial lung disease, and a mild form of epidermolysis bullosa. In mice with targeted deletion of integrin α3, the kidney and skin basement membranes are disorganized and mild blistering occurs; specifically, the lamina densa appears normal beneath hemidesmosomes but is missing or sparse between them. [Chapter: 28 The Biology of the Basement Membrane, p.629]
chapter: 28 The Biology of the Basement Membrane

question: What is the mechanism of action of topical capsaicin, and what practical considerations (application, onset of effect, side effects) are important for its use?
answer: Capsaicin activates the TRPV1 vanilloid receptor (which also responds to temperatures >43°C/109°F), causing repeated release of substance P from C neurons that eventually depletes this neuropeptide and reduces transmission of heat, pain, and itch. It is applied three to five times daily (or as a single 1-hour application of the 8% patch), initially causing a warmth/burning sensation, with therapeutic effect beginning about 1 week after starting treatment. Burning, stinging, and/or erythema occur at the application site in more than 50% of patients, so hand washing after application is recommended to prevent irritation of unaffected skin, eyes, and mucosal surfaces. [Chapter: 129 Other Topical Medications, p.2763]

question: According to this excerpt, what is the proposed mechanism by which topical capsaicin relieves conditions like postherpetic neuralgia and diabetic neuropathy, and what practical concern limits its use on certain skin?
answer: Capsaicin binds to the vanilloid receptor-1 on pain fibers, stimulating release and eventual depletion of the neurotransmitter substance P; prolonged exposure deactivates these neurons, providing pain relief. However, it commonly causes stinging and burning sensations, which can be especially unpleasant when applied to fissured or denuded skin, so it should be used with caution in these areas. [Chapter: 133 Complementary and Alternative Medicine, p.2825]

question: A patient who snorts cocaine presents with retiform purpura with ulceration, neutropenia, and positive ANCA (including anti-PR3) and anti-dsDNA autoantibodies. What substance adulterating the cocaine is responsible for this presentation, and what other systemic symptoms may accompany it?
answer: Cocaine adulterated with levamisole is responsible for this presentation, which can occur with snorting or IV use, and also with smoking crack cocaine adulterated with levamisole. In addition to retiform purpura with ulceration, neutropenia/leukopenia, and autoantibodies (ANA, ANCAs including anti-PR3 and elastase, anti-dsDNA, lupus anticoagulant), patients may develop arthralgias, pulmonary hemorrhage, seizures, and glomerulonephritis. [Chapter: 89 Signs of Substance Use Disorder, p.1947-1948]

question: In a patient with stasis dermatitis who develops secondary autosensitization (id) dermatitis due to contact sensitization, what is the characteristic distribution pattern of the resulting eczematous patches?
answer: The eczematous patches arise in a strikingly symmetric distribution, particularly affecting the anterior aspect of the contralateral leg, the anterior thighs, and the extensor surfaces of the upper extremities. In more severe cases, the lesions may generalize to involve the trunk and face as well. [Chapter: 13 Other Eczematous Eruptions, p.316]

question: For actinic keratosis treatment with methyl-ALA PDT, what two modifications to the standard protocol have been shown to reduce cutaneous inflammation while maintaining equivalent efficacy, and what is the difference in mALA application time compared to the recommended duration?
answer: Reduced cutaneous inflammation with equivalent efficacy was achieved by applying mALA for only 30 minutes instead of the recommended 3 hours, and/or by pretreating the skin with superpotent topical corticosteroids before PDT. [Chapter: 135 Photodynamic Therapy, p.2860]

question: What clinical, laboratory, and outcome features distinguish Harlequin ichthyosis (caused by ABCA12 or KDSR mutations) from typical autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis?
answer: Harlequin ichthyosis presents at birth with very thick, yellow–brown plates of scale that tightly encase the neonate, along with large, deep, bright red fissures; survivors go on to develop a severe CIE-like phenotype with palmoplantar keratoderma. It is associated with premature delivery and often neonatal death from sepsis or respiratory insufficiency, extreme ectropion, eclabium, and ear deformities, and later heat intolerance, skin infections, growth delay, joint contractures/arthritis, and thrombocytopenia (the latter specifically with KDSR mutations). Diagnosis is made clinically. [Chapter: 57 Ichthyoses, Erythrokeratodermas, and Related Disorders, p.1100-1101]

question: How do inactivating mutations in PTCH1 versus activating mutations in SMO each lead to constitutive activation of GLI and downstream target genes in basal cell carcinoma?
answer: Normally, Hedgehog binding to Patched (PTCH) removes repression of Smoothened (SMO), allowing signal transduction via GLI to the nucleus. Inactivating mutations in PTCH1 result in a dysfunctional Patched protein that mimics Hedgehog binding, thereby constitutively activating GLI and its downstream targets. Alternatively, an activating mutation in SMO itself causes constitutive signaling to GLI and downstream genes independent of PTCH1 status; such SMO mutations are found in sporadic BCCs where PTCH1 is intact. [Chapter: 108 Actinic Keratosis, Basal Cell Carcinoma, and Squamous Cell Carcinoma, p.2306-2308]
chapter: 108 Actinic Keratosis, Basal Cell Carcinoma, and Squamous Cell Carcinoma

question: In CHILD syndrome, what characteristic distribution and clinical features distinguish the cutaneous erythema and hyperkeratotic plaques, and what associated ipsilateral abnormalities may be seen?
answer: The erythema most often affects the right side of the body and is sharply demarcated at the anterior and posterior midline, typically sparing the face; during infancy it lessens as hyperkeratotic, verrucous plaques or bands develop, sometimes following Blaschko's lines and favoring skin folds (ptychotropism). Ipsilateral findings include linear alopecia, claw-like nail dystrophy or onychorrhexis, and skeletal abnormalities ranging from digit or rib hypoplasia to complete amelia, along with possible scoliosis and asymmetric hypoplasia of the brain, kidneys, heart, and lungs on the affected side. [Chapter: 57 Ichthyoses, Erythrokeratodermas, and Related Disorders, p.1127-1128]

question: In ataxia–telangiectasia, where do the oculocutaneous telangiectasias first appear, at what age, and what do the non-facial cutaneous telangiectasias typically resemble?
answer: The telangiectasias first appear at 3–6 years of age on the lateral and medial bulbar conjunctivae as red, symmetric horizontal streaks. They subsequently develop on other areas such as the popliteal fossae and presternal area, and less commonly on the dorsal hands/feet and hard/soft palate. The non-facial cutaneous telangiectasias are often subtle, resembling fine petechiae. [Chapter: 60 Primary Immunodeficiencies, p.1177]

question: How can REM (reticular erythematous mucinosis) be histologically distinguished from lupus erythematosus tumidus, given that both show perivascular T-cell infiltrates and increased dermal mucin?
answer: In REM, the mucin deposits and lymphocytic infiltrate tend to be located more superficially in the dermis and the lymphocytes appear more scattered, whereas in LE tumidus the infiltrate is somewhat deeper. Additionally, plasmacytoid dendritic cells are clustered in LE tumidus but are fewer and appear as single cells in REM. Despite these differences, some authors consider REM and LE tumidus to represent variants of the same disease along a continuum with cutaneous LE. [Chapter: 46 Mucinoses, p.944-945]

question: Why is warfarin associated with an increased risk of calciphylaxis, and why does chronic renal disease also increase this risk?
answer: Vitamin K2 (metaquinone) is stored in vessels and bones and is required for carboxylation of vascular calcification inhibitors, particularly Gas6 and matrix Gla protein (MGP). Chronic renal disease depletes vascular vitamin K2 stores, impairing carboxylation of these inhibitors and accelerating arterial and presumably cutaneous vessel calcification. Warfarin, as a vitamin K antagonist, further interferes with K2-dependent carboxylation of Gas6 and MGP, compounding this risk and explaining its association with calciphylaxis. [Chapter: 23 Cutaneous Manifestations of Microvascular Occlusion Syndromes, p.523]
chapter: 23 Cutaneous Manifestations of Microvascular Occlusion Syndromes

question: How does the sensitivity of Gram-stained smears for diagnosing gonorrhea differ between symptomatic men and women, and why are smears not useful for detecting rectal or pharyngeal gonorrhea?
answer: Gram-stained urethral exudate detects 95%–98% of symptomatic gonococcal infections in men, whereas Gram-stained cervical smears in women have a much lower sensitivity of about 50%. Smears are not helpful for rectal and pharyngeal gonorrhea because these sites harbor large numbers of other bacteria that interfere with identification of the Gram-negative diplococci. [Chapter: 82 Sexually Transmitted Infections, p.1786]

question: How do dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria (DSH) and dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria (DUH) differ in terms of distribution and underlying genetics?
answer: DSH presents with symmetrical hyper- and hypopigmented macules confined to the distal extremities, especially the dorsal hands and feet, sparing the palms, soles, and mucous membranes; it is caused by heterozygous mutations in ADAR, which encodes an RNA-specific adenosine deaminase. DUH, in contrast, causes truncal or generalized hyper- and hypopigmented macules that can involve the palms and soles (but not mucous membranes), and is caused by mutations in ABCB6 (an ATP-binding cassette transporter) or SASH1. Both conditions usually present by age 6 and are most common in Japan. [Chapter: 67 Disorders of Hyperpigmentation, p.1391-1392]

question: Among posaconazole, isavuconazole, and voriconazole, which have activity against Mucormycetes, and which one is specifically approved for treatment of invasive mucormycosis?
answer: Posaconazole and isavuconazole both have activity against Mucormycetes (unlike voriconazole), and isavuconazole is specifically approved for the treatment of invasive mucormycosis. Voriconazole, by contrast, is superior for invasive Aspergillus infections but does not cover Mucormycetes. [Chapter: 77 Fungal Diseases, p.1657]

question: In classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS), what is the Gorlin sign, how prevalent is it among affected individuals compared to the general population, and what cardiac findings may also be associated with this EDS type?
answer: The Gorlin sign is the ability to touch the tip of the nose with the tongue, and it is present in at least half of individuals with classical EDS compared to only about 10% of the general population. Classical EDS may also be associated with mild aortic root dilation and mitral valve prolapse, each occurring in about 5% of patients, though these cardiac findings are rarely of clinical significance. [Chapter: 97 Heritable Disorders of Connective Tissue, p.2070-2071]

question: According to the excerpt, how do the natural courses of cutaneous LP and oral LP differ in terms of spontaneous remission, and how is a diagnosis of lichenoid drug eruption confirmed?
answer: Cutaneous LP often remits spontaneously, with up to two-thirds of patients clearing within 1 year, whereas oral LP has a much longer mean duration of about 5 years, and the erosive form of oral LP rarely resolves spontaneously. A lichenoid drug eruption is confirmed by withdrawing the suspected drug and observing gradual disappearance of the lesions, followed by recurrence of lesions upon re-exposure to the drug, though rechallenge is often not performed in practice. [Chapter: 11 Lichen Planus and Lichenoid Dermatoses, p.268-269]

question: When is a combination closure technique (using multiple flaps, or a flap plus a graft) preferred over a single flap for defect repair?
answer: Combination closures are used when a defect cannot be conveniently closed with a single flap—either because the defect is too large, or because it spans more than one cosmetic subunit. In large defects, a flap may close most of the wound while a full-thickness graft supplements it to complete coverage; grafts can be harvested from common donor sites based on tissue match. For defects crossing multiple cosmetic subunits, it is often best to repair each subunit individually with a different flap. [Chapter: 147 Flaps, p.3043-3044]

question: In lipodermatosclerosis, how do the clinical features of the acute phase differ from those of the chronic phase?
answer: In the acute phase, lipodermatosclerosis presents with pain, warmth, erythema, and relatively diffuse induration, typically starting on the medial lower leg above the malleolus (though other dependent sites like the lower abdominal pannus can be affected). In the chronic phase, there is marked sclerosis of the dermis and subcutis producing induration that is more sharply demarcated from surrounding normal skin, often with brown hemosiderin discoloration, giving the leg an inverted wine bottle appearance. [Chapter: 100 Panniculitis, p.2128]

question: According to the diagnostic criteria for cutaneous mastocytosis, what major criterion and which minor criteria must be met to establish the diagnosis in skin?
answer: The major criterion is the presence of clinically typical skin lesions of mastocytosis associated with a positive Darier sign. This must be combined with at least one of two minor criteria: (1) an increased number of mast cells in lesional skin, or (2) detection of an activating KIT mutation in lesional skin. [Chapter: 118 Mastocytosis, p.2576-2577]

question: What clinical features characterize pincer nails, what condition should be excluded by X-ray, what systemic drugs might suggest a drug-induced etiology, and what is the treatment of choice?
answer: Pincer nails show excessive transverse overcurvature of the nail plate, especially distally, which compresses (pinches) the distal nail bed and can cause severe pain; they are usually seen on the toes and may be hereditary or acquired (often from ill-fitting shoes). Subungual exostosis should be excluded by X-ray examination. Drug-induced pincer nails (e.g., from β-blockers) should be considered when several nails, including fingernails, are involved. The treatment of choice is lateral chemical or surgical matricectomy. [Chapter: 71 Nail Disorders, p.1483]

question: How does the pattern of acantholysis in Hailey–Hailey disease (HHD) differ from that seen in Darier disease, and what histologic feature helps distinguish HHD from pemphigus vulgaris or pemphigoid vegetans?
answer: In Darier disease, acantholysis occurs primarily within discrete foci, whereas in HHD it is more widespread throughout the epidermis, producing larger areas of dyscohesion described as a "dilapidated brick wall," with dermal papillae ("villi") protruding into blister cavities and rare necrotic or dyskeratotic cells compared to Darier disease. HHD is distinguished from pemphigus vulgaris and pemphigoid vegetans by direct immunofluorescence (DIF), which is negative in HHD but positive in these autoimmune blistering diseases. [Chapter: 59 Darier Disease and Hailey–Hailey Disease, p.1173-1174]

question: In a neonate or infant with suspected ichthyosis, what specific laboratory or biopsy-based test would you use to evaluate for (a) neutral lipid storage disease and (b) Sjögren–Larsson syndrome?
answer: For suspected neutral lipid storage disease, lipid antibodies such as adipophilin, or stains such as oil red O or Sudan III, can be used to detect cytoplasmic lipid droplets in paraffin-embedded or fresh frozen skin sections, respectively. For suspected Sjögren–Larsson syndrome, fibroblast or keratinocyte cultures from a skin biopsy specimen can be used to measure FALDH activity or check for elevated free fatty alcohols. [Chapter: 57 Ichthyoses, Erythrokeratodermas, and Related Disorders, p.1106-1107]

question: Why is fluconazole particularly well-suited for treating fungal meningitis compared to other systemic azole antifungals, and what infection is it generally considered the drug of choice for?
answer: Fluconazole is relatively hydrophilic compared to other systemic azole antifungal drugs, which allows it to be distributed into the cerebrospinal fluid, making it useful for treating fungal meningitis. It is also generally considered the drug of choice for systemic candidiasis, although fungemia due to azole-resistant Candida can occur. [Chapter: 127 Antimicrobial Drugs, p.2723-2724]

question: According to this excerpt, how does onabotulinumtoxinA (BTA) treat hyperhidrosis, how long does its effect last, and what is a notable side effect along with its course?
answer: OnabotulinumtoxinA works by preventing the release of acetylcholine from cholinergic neurons; when injected into hyperhidrotic skin, it produces near anhidrosis lasting 4 to 6 months. A notable side effect is muscle weakness, especially of the intrinsic muscles of the hands or feet, which resolves spontaneously over 2 to 5 weeks. Compensatory hyperhidrosis has not been observed with this treatment. [Chapter: 39 Diseases of the Eccrine and Apocrine Sweat Glands, p.810]
chapter: 39 Diseases of the Eccrine and Apocrine Sweat Glands

question: Why can a Staphylococcus aureus isolate that appears susceptible to clindamycin on initial testing (but resistant to erythromycin) still fail clindamycin therapy, and how is this phenomenon detected in the laboratory?
answer: If the isolate carries an erm gene (encoding erythromycin ribosomal methylase), exposure to erythromycin induces erm expression, which also confers cross-resistance to clindamycin. Even if initial testing shows erythromycin resistance but clindamycin susceptibility, bacterial variants with constitutive erm expression commonly emerge during clindamycin therapy and are selected for, leading to clinical resistance. This "inducible resistance" can be assessed using the D-test (double-disk diffusion). [Chapter: 74 Bacterial Diseases, p.1547]

question: According to the historical overview of cutaneous T cell lymphoma, who first described mycosis fungoides, in what year, and what was the original name given to the condition?
answer: Mycosis fungoides was first described in 1806 by the French physician Jean Louis Alibert, who designated the case as "pian fungoïde" in his atlas. It was later renamed mycosis fungoides in 1835 because some of the skin tumors resembled mushrooms. [Chapter: 120 Cutaneous T Cell Lymphoma, p.2602-2603]

question: In a biopsy of mycetoma showing tightly packed fungal grains, how can histopathology help distinguish eumycotic from actinomycotic subtypes?
answer: The distinction is made by comparing the diameter of the filaments composing the grain to the size of the nuclei of surrounding inflammatory cells: eumycotic mycetomas have thicker filaments, while actinomycotic mycetomas have thin, fine filaments. Special stains such as methenamine silver or Brown–Brenn can further aid in differentiating the subtype. [Chapter: 77 Fungal Diseases, p.1646]

question: What is the most common clinical presentation of chronic Q fever, and what are some cutaneous manifestations that have been described in Q fever?
answer: Chronic Q fever most often presents as "culture-negative" endocarditis affecting a previously damaged heart valve. Although cutaneous manifestations of Q fever are rare, reported findings include a truncal maculopapular rash, an urticarial eruption, erythema nodosum, palpable purpura, palatal petechiae, and vasculitis (the latter associated with mixed cryoglobulinemia). [Chapter: 76 Rickettsial Diseases, p.1625-1626]

question: By definition, how is linear IgA bullous dermatosis (LABD) distinguished from dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) and bullous pemphigoid (BP) using direct immunofluorescence (DIF)?
answer: LABD is characterized by linear IgA deposition along the basement membrane zone (BMZ) in perilesional skin. This differs from DH, which shows granular deposition of IgA in the dermal papillary tips or in a continuous pattern along the basement membrane, and from BP, which shows linear deposition of IgG (not IgA) along the epidermal BMZ. [Chapter: 31 Dermatitis Herpetiformis and Linear IgA Bullous Dermatosis, p.683-684]
chapter: 31 Dermatitis Herpetiformis and Linear IgA B­ullous Dermatosis

question: For a patient with acne keloidalis nuchae, how should surgical management differ between a plaque with a vertical diameter of 1.0–1.5 cm versus one greater than 1.5 cm, and why?
answer: For plaques 1.0–1.5 cm in vertical diameter, excision with primary closure (extending below the base of the hair follicles) is the treatment of choice. For lesions greater than 1.5 cm in vertical diameter, primary closure should be avoided because the postoperative scar tends to spread to the width of the excisional defect, producing a hairless flat scar; instead, these larger lesions should be excised to the level of the fascia or deep subcutaneous tissue and allowed to heal by second intention, a process that typically takes 8–12 weeks. [Chapter: 38 Folliculitis, Follicular Occlusion Tetrad, and Other Follicular Disorders, p.792]
chapter: 38 Folliculitis, Follicular Occlusion Tetrad, and Other Follicular Disorders

question: Why has DNA-based testing using chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis largely replaced fetal skin biopsy for prenatal diagnosis of genodermatoses, and what is a key requirement for approaches like non-invasive prenatal testing and preimplantation genetic diagnosis?
answer: DNA-based testing via chorionic villus sampling (8–10 weeks' EGA) or amniocentesis (12–14 weeks' EGA) has largely replaced fetal skin biopsy because it can be performed earlier in pregnancy and poses less risk to the mother and fetus than skin biopsy, which was traditionally done at 19–22 weeks' EGA. For non-invasive prenatal testing (using circulating fetal cells or cell-free DNA) and preimplantation genetic diagnosis, the pathogenic mutation(s) must first be identified in family members before prenatal testing can be performed. [Chapter: 2 Skin Development and Maintenance, p.104]

question: According to this excerpt, what histologic features suggest that a skin lesion represents a bite or sting reaction?
answer: Suggestive histologic features include a wedge-shaped perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with eosinophils, endothelial prominence, and overlying spongiosis or focal epidermal necrosis. Marked spongiosis can progress to blister formation, and Langerhans cell hyperplasia may also be present. [Chapter: 85 Bites and Stings, p.1856]

question: Why is it important for a clinician to ask a patient about the use of traditional practices such as moxibustion, cupping, or skin scraping (coining) before suspecting abuse when they observe skin lesions with patterns suggestive of an external cause?
answer: These practices can produce skin findings that mimic signs of abuse: moxibustion can cause first- and second-degree burns, cupping can leave circular areas of erythema and ecchymosis, and skin scraping (coining/spooning) can cause symmetric, linear ecchymoses. Because these traditional treatments are common (e.g., coining is widely practiced in Southeast Asia) and can create externally patterned lesions, patients should be asked about such practices before accusations of abuse are made. [Chapter: 133 Complementary and Alternative Medicine, p.2829-2830]

question: According to global burden of disease data from 2013, how significant was the impact of skin diseases in terms of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), and how common are dermatologic conditions in outpatient care in the US?
answer: Based on 2013 global burden of disease data, skin diseases accounted for over 41 million DALYs lost and ranked as the fourth most common cause of non-fatal disease burden worldwide. In the US, dermatology represents about 4% of all outpatient visits, making it the third most common subspecialty ambulatory visit after ophthalmology and orthopedics, with additional visits for skin conditions occurring in primary care (5%-8%) and emergency departments (4%). [Chapter: 123 Public Health and Dermatology, p.2654-2655]

question: How can loricrin keratoderma be clinically distinguished from Vohwinkel syndrome, given that both present with a honeycomb-pattern keratoderma, pseudoainhum, knuckle pads, and warty extensor keratoses?
answer: Loricrin keratoderma is distinguished from Vohwinkel syndrome by the absence of deafness and the presence of ichthyosis in loricrin keratoderma, whereas Vohwinkel syndrome (caused by GJB2/connexin 26 mutations) is associated with sensorineural deafness. [Chapter: 58 Palmoplantar Keratodermas, p.1150]

question: What is the approved adalimumab dosing regimen for treating hidradenitis suppurativa in adult and adolescent patients weighing ≥60 kg, and how does this differ for adolescents weighing 30–59 kg?
answer: For adults and adolescents weighing ≥60 kg, adalimumab is given as a 160 mg loading dose, followed by 80 mg on day 15, and then either 40 mg weekly or 80 mg every other week starting on day 29. For adolescent HS patients weighing 30–59 kg, the regimen consists of an 80 mg loading dose followed by 40 mg every other week starting on day 8. [Chapter: 128 Systemic Immunomodulators, p.2741-2742]

question: How does the histopathologic processing of tissue in Mohs micrographic surgery differ from that used in standard surgical excisions?
answer: In MMS, the excised tissue disc (layer) is cryopreserved and cut in a horizontal fashion, then mounted on slides, stained, and examined microscopically for residual tumor, allowing evaluation of the entire 360° circumferential margin. In contrast, standard excision specimens are formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) and cut in a "bread-loaf" fashion, which does not provide complete margin examination. [Chapter: 150 Mohs Micrographic Surgery, p.3078]

question: Why should a biopsy specimen for suspected erosive lichen planus include the edge of the erosion along with the surrounding lacy reticulated skin, and what is the value of histologic evaluation in this setting?
answer: Because erosive lichen planus involves loss of the epithelium within the erosion itself, a specimen from the erosion alone would not capture diagnostic features; including the edge of the erosion plus adjacent lacy reticulated skin gives the best chance of showing characteristic changes. Even so, histology cannot always unequivocally confirm lichen planus, but it remains useful for excluding other entities in the differential diagnosis, such as autoimmune bullous disease, Zoon vulvitis, or HSIL/SCC. [Chapter: 73 Anogenital (Non-venereal) Diseases, p.1525]

question: In Naegeli–Franceschetti–Jadassohn (NFJ) syndrome, how do truncating mutations in KRT14 lead to the characteristic reticulated hyperpigmentation seen histologically?
answer: NFJ syndrome results from truncating mutations in the non-helical head domain of KRT14, causing haploinsufficiency. This increases keratinocyte susceptibility to TNF-induced apoptosis, leading to pigment incontinence—seen histologically as melanophages in the upper dermis—which produces the clinical reticulated hyperpigmentation. [Chapter: 67 Disorders of Hyperpigmentation, p.1388]

question: What overlapping clinical and histologic features between lymphomatoid papulosis (LyP) and cutaneous anaplastic large cell lymphoma (C-ALCL) support classifying LyP as a low-grade variant of CTCL rather than a purely benign condition?
answer: LyP and C-ALCL share overlapping clinical and histologic features, including the presence of an aberrant T cell phenotype, clonally rearranged TCR genes in 60%–70% of LyP patients, and identical T cell clones found in LyP lesions and associated lymphoma lesions. Because of these shared features, LyP is best regarded as a low-grade variant of CTCL rather than simply a benign or premalignant process. [Chapter: 120 Cutaneous T Cell Lymphoma, p.2615-2616]

question: How can granuloma faciale be distinguished from erythema elevatum diutinum (EED) based on clinical distribution and histopathologic findings, and what first-line treatments are recommended for granuloma faciale?
answer: EED presents as multiple red-brown papules, plaques, or nodules in a symmetric distribution on the extensor extremities with a predilection for skin overlying joints, whereas granuloma faciale is typically facial. Histopathologically, EED shows more pronounced fibrosis and lipid-laden macrophages, which are not seen in granuloma faciale. First-line treatments for granuloma faciale include topical or intralesional corticosteroids (e.g., triamcinolone suspension 2.5-5 mg/ml) and topical calcineurin inhibitors (pimecrolimus, tacrolimus), often requiring 3-6 months of therapy for improvement. [Chapter: 24 Cutaneous Vasculitis, p.547]

question: What are the key clinical, trichoscopic, and histopathologic features of lipedematous scalp/alopecia, and what treatments have shown partial hair regrowth in case reports?
answer: Lipedematous scalp presents as a soft, 'spongy' scalp that pits with finger pressure, due to lymphatic dilatation and edematous thickening of the subcutis and dermis; when hair loss is present (lipedematous alopecia), hairs are sparse and short (~1-2 cm). Trichoscopy shows multiple thin and vellus hairs plus linear erythema with fine arborizing vessels, while histopathology reveals roughly doubled scalp thickness from subcutaneous fat expansion, and in prominent alopecia, replacement of hair follicles with fibrous tracts without notable inflammation. Case reports describe partial hair regrowth with topical clobetasol, intralesional triamcinolone, or mycophenolate mofetil. [Chapter: 69 Alopecias, p.1431]

question: How is essential fatty acid (EFA) deficiency diagnosed biochemically, and under what circumstances can an isolated EFA deficiency occur?
answer: EFA deficiency is diagnosed by finding decreased plasma levels of linoleic and linolenic acids together with increased levels of eicosatrienoic acid, which is normally undetectable. An isolated EFA deficiency is uncommon but can occur with parenteral nutrition lacking lipid supplementation or with overly aggressive low-fat diets; more often, however, EFA deficiency occurs alongside other nutritional deficiencies. [Chapter: 51 Nutritional Diseases, p.1003-1004]

question: For a patient with NOMID and renal impairment (creatinine clearance < 30 mL/min) being treated with anakinra, what dosing adjustment is recommended, and what laboratory monitoring should be performed given anakinra's major side effects?
answer: In NOMID patients with creatinine clearance < 30 mL/min, anakinra should be given every other day rather than daily. Because neutropenia and thrombocytopenia are potentially serious side effects, complete blood counts should be monitored monthly for the first 3 months of therapy and then quarterly thereafter. [Chapter: 128 Systemic Immunomodulators, p.2746]

question: According to the TNMB classification of mycosis fungoides/Sézary syndrome, what laboratory criteria must be met for a patient's blood involvement to be classified as B2 (high blood tumor burden)?
answer: B2 requires that the patient be clone positive, plus meet at least one of the following: an absolute Sézary cell count of ≥1000/mcl, a CD4/CD8 ratio >10, CD4+CD7− cells ≥40%, or CD4+CD26− cells ≥30%. This distinguishes B2 from B1 (low blood tumor burden, clone positive but not meeting these thresholds) and B0 (absence of significant blood involvement, <5% atypical Sézary cells). [Chapter: 120 Cutaneous T Cell Lymphoma, p.2608-2609]

question: According to the excerpt, what are the indications for systemic chemotherapy in Kaposi sarcoma (KS), and which agents are commonly used?
answer: Systemic chemotherapy is indicated for rapidly progressive KS (defined as 10 or more new cutaneous lesions per month), pulmonary KS, symptomatic visceral involvement, and significant lymphedema. Liposomal anthracyclines, paclitaxel, and vinblastine are used singly or in combination, with vincristine, gemcitabine, vinorelbine, etoposide, and/or bleomycin used less often. [Chapter: 114 Vascular Neoplasms and Neoplastic-Like Proliferations, p.2491-2492]

question: According to the lipid-lowering medications table, what is the mechanism of action of ANGPTL3 inhibitors such as evinacumab, and what specific patient population is this drug class used to treat?
answer: ANGPTL3 inhibitors like evinacumab bind to ANGPTL3, a protein expressed mainly in the liver that normally inhibits lipoprotein lipase and endothelial lipase; by blocking ANGPTL3, these drugs rescue the activity of these enzymes and promote VLDL processing and clearance upstream of LDL formation, lowering LDL-C (independent of LDL receptor presence), HDL-C, and triglycerides. They are used to treat homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia and are administered intravenously in combination with other lipid-lowering drugs such as statins or PCSK9 inhibitors. [Chapter: 92 Xanthomas, p.1997-2000]

question: Through which chemokine receptor do eotaxins 1, 2, and 3 (CCL11, CCL24, and CCL26) primarily signal to attract eosinophils, and what additional effect do these chemokines have besides chemotaxis?
answer: Eotaxins 1, 2, and 3 signal primarily through C-C chemokine receptor (CCR)-3, which is highly expressed on eosinophils. In addition to their chemotactic properties, these chemokines also induce the release of reactive oxygen species. [Chapter: 26 Eosinophil-Associated Dermatoses, p.592]

question: According to Happle's classification, what are the seven patterns of cutaneous mosaicism, and which one has not yet been shown to be mosaic at the molecular level in any condition?
answer: Happle categorized cutaneous mosaicism into seven patterns: (1,2) narrow or broad bands along the lines of Blaschko; (3) checkerboard (block- or flag-like); (4) lateralization (affecting only one side of the body); (5) phylloid (leaf- or flower-like); (6) patchy without midline separation; and (7) sash. Of these, all except the sash pattern have been confirmed to be mosaic at the molecular level in at least one condition. [Chapter: 62 Mosaicism and Linear Lesions, p.1235]

question: According to the excerpt, what allergens caused allergic contact dermatitis in the salon technician, and at what body site was involvement noted?
answer: The salon technician had allergic contact dermatitis to 2-hydroxyethylmethacrylate (HEMA), found in nail polish, and to nickel. The excerpt specifically notes involvement of the fingertip. [Chapter: 14 Allergic Contact Dermatitis, p.331-332]

question: Why does electrofulguration produce only very superficial tissue destruction, and why is it not the preferred waveform when hemostasis during surgical excision is needed?
answer: Electrofulguration works by holding the electrode at a slight distance from the tissue so a spark jumps to the surface, causing surface carbonization that insulates underlying tissue from thermal heat spread, resulting in very superficial destruction. Because the electrical current does not penetrate deeply enough to seal nearby blood vessels, blood can appear in droplets through the surface char, so electrocoagulation is a better current choice than electrofulguration when hemostasis is required during surgical excision. [Chapter: 140 Electrosurgery, p.2924]

question: Which patient group with congenital melanocytic nevi is at the greatest risk for neurocutaneous melanosis, and what is the reported risk percentage in one study?
answer: Patients who present with multiple medium-sized congenital nevi in the absence of a large congenital nevus are at the greatest risk for neurocutaneous melanosis, with one study reporting a risk of up to 70%. [Chapter: 112 Benign Melanocytic Neoplasms and Melanotic Lesions, p.2406]
chapter: 112 Benign Melanocytic Neoplasms and Melanotic Lesions

question: In the treatment of intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP), what is the therapeutic goal, which agent is recommended to achieve it, and what is its recommended dosing regimen?
answer: Because fetal prognosis correlates with disease severity, the therapeutic goal in ICP is to reduce serum bile acid levels, which prolongs pregnancy and lessens fetal risk and maternal symptoms. Oral ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) is the only agent shown to be successful, dosed at 15 mg/kg daily or, independent of body weight, 1 g daily, started as early as possible and continued until delivery. It is safe for mother and fetus, with mild diarrhea as its only side effect, though its use is off-label since it is only approved for primary biliary cirrhosis. [Chapter: 27 Pregnancy Dermatoses, p.609]

question: According to the excerpt, in patients with good skin quality, is device-assisted liposuction necessary compared to manual liposuction, and why?
answer: No, in individuals with good skin quality, device-assisted liposuction devices are likely unnecessary because manual liposuction alone already provides good skin contraction. These devices offer their major advantage—skin tightening—primarily in patients with more skin laxity or fibrous tissue, and they also carry increased costs, including disposable costs. [Chapter: 156 Body Contouring: Liposuction and Non-invasive Modalities, p.3179]
chapter: 156 Body Contouring: Liposuction and Non-invasive Modalities

question: According to the differential diagnosis of cutaneous microvascular occlusion based on pathophysiology, name two categories that include cold-related mechanisms and vessel-invasive organisms, and give two examples from each category.
answer: The category "Cold-related precipitation or agglutination" includes examples such as cryoglobulinemia (type I) and cryofibrinogenemia (or cold agglutinins). The category "Vessel-invasive organisms" includes examples such as ecthyma gangrenosum (primarily Gram-negative bacteria) and opportunistic fungi (e.g. Aspergillus spp., Rhizopus spp.), among others like disseminated strongyloidiasis, Lucio phenomenon, and Rickettsia spp. [Chapter: 23 Cutaneous Manifestations of Microvascular Occlusion Syndromes, p.508-509]
chapter: 23 Cutaneous Manifestations of Microvascular Occlusion Syndromes

question: Why is topical antibiotic monotherapy (e.g., clindamycin or erythromycin) generally not recommended for the treatment of acne?
answer: Because C. acnes commonly develops resistance to clindamycin and erythromycin, with resistance rates exceeding 50% in some countries, topical antibiotic monotherapy is not generally recommended for acne treatment. Instead, these antibiotics are typically used in combination with benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid. [Chapter: 36 Acne Vulgaris, p.755]

question: What does the acronym PIBIDS stand for in describing findings associated with trichothiodystrophy types 1–3, and how do TTD1–3 differ from TTD4–9?
answer: PIBIDS stands for Photosensitivity, Ichthyosis, Brittle hair, Intellectual impairment with low IQ, Decreased fertility, and Short stature. TTD1–3 are associated with photosensitivity (and are reviewed in Table 87.4), whereas TTD4–9, including X-linked recessive TTD5, do not have photosensitivity. Some patients may also show spasticity, tremors, ataxia, nail dystrophy, dental caries, cataracts, and bony and immune defects, and the hair abnormality usually does not improve with age. [Chapter: 69 Alopecias, p.1438-1439]

question: In a woman with PCOS who is at higher risk for VTE (e.g., obesity, age ≥40 years), what type of combined OCP formulation is recommended, and why should levonorgestrel-containing cOCPs be avoided in this population?
answer: For women at higher VTE risk, the recommended cOCP should contain the lowest effective dose of ethinyl estradiol (usually 20 mcg) combined with a low VTE-risk progestin such as norgestimate or norethindrone. Levonorgestrel, although associated with low VTE risk, is the most androgenic progestin and may have adverse metabolic effects, making it less suitable for patients with PCOS. [Chapter: 70 Hypertrichosis and Hirsutism, p.1463]

question: In levamisole-induced vasculopathy, what laboratory finding pattern helps distinguish this condition from a primary ANCA-associated vasculitis?
answer: Levamisole-induced vasculopathy is associated with a high rate of ANCA positivity (~95%), but isolated cANCA positivity occurs in fewer than 5% of patients, with most having both anti-myeloperoxidase and anti-proteinase antibodies. Because of this, the finding of cANCA positivity alone is unusual for levamisole-induced vasculopathy and should raise strong suspicion for a primary ANCA-associated vasculitis instead. [Chapter: 23 Cutaneous Manifestations of Microvascular Occlusion Syndromes, p.523]
chapter: 23 Cutaneous Manifestations of Microvascular Occlusion Syndromes

question: What are the three major dermoscopic patterns seen in acral nevi, and what are the typical histopathologic features of the junctional and dermal components of these nevi?
answer: The three major dermoscopic patterns in acral nevi are the parallel furrow pattern, the lattice-like pattern, and the fibrillar pattern. Histologically, acral nevi are usually small (<5–6 mm), well-circumscribed, symmetric compound nevi with junctional nests that are fairly uniform in round or oval shape and similar in size and spacing (though occasionally somewhat enlarged), often showing lentiginous melanocytic proliferation and some upward migration of melanocytes. The dermal component is often characterized by round nests of melanocytes. [Chapter: 112 Benign Melanocytic Neoplasms and Melanotic Lesions, p.2396-2397]
chapter: 112 Benign Melanocytic Neoplasms and Melanotic Lesions

question: A patient presents with hirsutism. How can laboratory findings help distinguish PCOS, ovarian hyperthecosis, and an androgen-secreting adrenal tumor from one another?
answer: In PCOS, testosterone is normal to elevated, DHEAS is normal, and the LH:FSH ratio is >3, with chronic anovulation and/or polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. Ovarian hyperthecosis shows markedly elevated testosterone (↑↑) with normal DHEAS, typically in postmenopausal women with progressive severe hirsutism/virilization. An androgen-secreting adrenal tumor shows elevated to markedly elevated testosterone along with markedly elevated DHEAS and elevated cortisol, presenting with rapid-onset hirsutism and virilization. [Chapter: 70 Hypertrichosis and Hirsutism, p.1458]

question: Why is polypropylene suture (e.g., Prolene) particularly well-suited for use as a running subcuticular suture, and what are its main disadvantages?
answer: Polypropylene has a low coefficient of friction that allows a gentle, smooth pull through tissue and permits easy withdrawal even after extended periods without disrupting the wound, making it ideal for running subcuticular closures. It also has high plasticity, stretching with tissue swelling to reduce postoperative track marks. Its main disadvantages are memory, which compromises knot security, and higher cost compared to nylon. [Chapter: 144 Wound Closure Materials and Instruments, p.2976]

question: What is the chemical irritant in Dieffenbachia picta ("dumb cane"), how does it cause symptoms when the leaves are chewed, and what is the recommended treatment?
answer: Dieffenbachia picta contains calcium oxalate, which is water-insoluble and released from the leaves upon contact with a moist surface. When the leaves are chewed, this causes salivation, burning, mucosal edema, and blistering, leading to hoarseness or aphonia (hence the name "dumb cane"). Treatment includes parenteral corticosteroids, antacid mouthwashes, and analgesics (antihistamines are not helpful), with pain and edema resolving over 4–12 days. [Chapter: 17 Dermatoses Due to Plants, p.384-385]

question: Which two skin sites, other than the nose (rhinophyma) and chin (gnathophyma), can be affected by phymatous changes in rosacea, and what happens to nasal contour in grade 2 (moderate) phymatous rosacea?
answer: In addition to rhinophyma (nose) and gnathophyma (chin), phymatous rosacea can also affect the forehead (metophyma), ears (otophyma), and eyelids (blepharophyma). In grade 2 phymatous disease, there is moderate swelling with moderately dilated patulous follicles and mild hypertrophy of sebaceous glands or connective tissue, causing a change in nasal contour but without a nodular component. [Chapter: 37 Rosacea and Related Disorders, p.767]

question: According to the table of chemical mediators of inflammation involved in wound healing, what actions are attributed to serotonin and complement?
answer: Serotonin acts to stimulate fibroblast proliferation and promote cross-linking of collagen molecules. Complement increases vascular permeability, enhances phagocytosis, promotes bacterial lysis, and activates mast cells and basophils. [Chapter: 141 Biology of Wound Healing, p.2941-2943]

question: According to the excerpt, which patient population is at higher risk for eczema vaccinatum following smallpox vaccination, and how does the clinical distribution of mpox lesions typically differ between clade I and clade IIb infections?
answer: Eczema vaccinatum is a possible adverse event of smallpox vaccination that occurs in patients with atopic dermatitis or Darier disease. For mpox, clade I infection tends to show a centrifugal distribution that often involves the palms and soles, whereas clade IIb favors the genital, perianal, and oropharyngeal sites of inoculation. [Chapter: 81 Other Viral Diseases, p.1754]

question: For treatment of acyclovir-resistant HSV in immunocompromised patients, what are the recommended foscarnet and cidofovir dosing regimens?
answer: Foscarnet is given as 40 mg/kg IV every 8–12 hours for 2–3 weeks or until all lesions are healed. Cidofovir can be used as a 1% cream or gel applied daily for 2–3 weeks, or for severe disease as 5 mg/kg IV weekly for 2 weeks then every other week, given together with probenecid. [Chapter: 80 Human Herpesviruses, p.1720]

question: Why does salicylic acid remain on the stratum corneum while α-hydroxy acids penetrate more deeply, and what practical effect does this have during a salicylic acid peel?
answer: Salicylic acid is oil-soluble, so it stays on the surface of the stratum corneum, whereas α-hydroxy acids are water-soluble and readily penetrate into the stratum corneum. Because salicylic acid is self-neutralizing, the peel ends with formation of white salicylic acid crystals on the skin; these crystals rinse off the surface but remain in the follicular ostia, providing a prolonged keratolytic effect. [Chapter: 153 Cosmetics and Cosmeceuticals, p.3134-3135]

question: What are café-noir spots, and with which two syndromes are they associated?
answer: Café-noir spots are hyperpigmented patches with a darker hue relative to the background skin than café-au-lait macules. They are seen in LEOPARD syndrome (Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines) and Carney complex. [Chapter: 112 Benign Melanocytic Neoplasms and Melanotic Lesions, p.2384]
chapter: 112 Benign Melanocytic Neoplasms and Melanotic Lesions

question: According to the excerpt, what response rate did combination therapy with calcipotriene 0.005% ointment plus 5% 5-FU cream (twice daily for four consecutive days) achieve in patients with actinic keratoses, and what overall response rates were reported for cemiplimab in locally advanced versus metastatic cutaneous SCC?
answer: Combination therapy with calcipotriene 0.005% ointment plus 5% 5-FU cream given twice daily for four consecutive days achieved an 88% response rate in patients with actinic keratoses. For cemiplimab in advanced cutaneous SCC, overall response rates were 44% for locally advanced disease and 45% for metastatic disease, which led to FDA approval for both indications. [Chapter: 108 Actinic Keratosis, Basal Cell Carcinoma, and Squamous Cell Carcinoma, p.2295-2296]
chapter: 108 Actinic Keratosis, Basal Cell Carcinoma, and Squamous Cell Carcinoma

question: According to the recommended surgical excision margin guidelines for primary cutaneous melanoma, what margins are recommended for melanoma in situ, and for invasive melanomas ≤1 mm, >1–2 mm, and >2 mm in thickness?
answer: For melanoma in situ, excision margins of 0.5–1.0 cm are recommended (with lentigo maligna type possibly requiring ≥1 cm for histologic clearance). For invasive melanoma ≤1 mm thick, a margin of 1.0 cm is recommended; for tumors >1–2 mm thick, margins of 1.0–2.0 cm; and for tumors >2 mm thick, a margin of 2.0 cm. [Chapter: 113 Melanoma, p.2450-2451]

question: According to Bolognia, when should broad-spectrum antimicrobial coverage such as vancomycin plus piperacillin/tazobactam, imipenem, or meropenem be used in the treatment of cellulitis, and what should be avoided during treatment?
answer: Broad-spectrum coverage (e.g., vancomycin plus piperacillin/tazobactam, imipenem, or meropenem) should be given to patients with severe non-purulent cellulitis who are immunocompromised, hypotensive, or showing rapid progression of disease; diabetic or decubitus ulcers complicated by cellulitis likewise require broad-spectrum coverage (e.g., piperacillin/tazobactam, or metronidazole plus ciprofloxacin if penicillin-allergic). NSAIDs should be avoided when treating cellulitis because they may mask the signs and symptoms of deeper necrotizing infections. [Chapter: 74 Bacterial Diseases, p.1555]

question: A patient presents with a painful genital ulcer that has a purulent base and soft, undermined edges, developing 3–10 days after exposure. Painful unilateral inguinal lymphadenitis is also present. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what organism causes it?
answer: This presentation is characteristic of chancroid, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. Chancroid has an incubation period of 3–10 days and produces painful ulcers with purulent bases and soft, undermined edges, often accompanied by painful inguinal lymphadenitis (unilateral in about 40% of men), which can progress to bubo formation and rupture. Diagnosis is confirmed by culture or PCR. [Chapter: 82 Sexually Transmitted Infections, p.1789-1790]

question: According to the excerpt, what are two clinical settings in which surgical excision of an infantile hemangioma during the proliferative phase may be appropriate?
answer: Early surgical excision during the proliferative phase may be appropriate for a function-threatening hemangioma (such as a periocular lesion blocking the visual axis or a lip lesion interfering with feeding or speech) that has failed to respond to pharmacologic therapy, or when pharmacologic therapy is believed to pose greater risk than surgery. It may also be appropriate for pedunculated lesions for which resection is inevitable, or small, persistently ulcerated lesions that have failed conservative therapy. [Chapter: 103 Infantile Hemangiomas, p.2181]

question: What is the underlying pathogenesis of scombroid poisoning, and which fish are typically implicated?
answer: Scombroid poisoning occurs when fish with high levels of free histidine in their muscle tissue (originally fish of the family Scombridae such as tuna and mackerel, but also mahi mahi, bluefish, marlin, bonito, amberjack, sardines, anchovies, herring, and swordfish) are improperly refrigerated, allowing bacterial histidine decarboxylase to convert histidine into histamine. Ingestion of this histamine-laden fish delivers a large histamine dose that causes prompt effects via histamine receptor binding, though other factors such as potentiation of histamine absorption, inhibition of its catabolism, an unidentified "scombrotoxin," and histamine intolerance may also contribute. [Chapter: 88 Environmental and Sports-Related Skin Diseases, p.1930-1931]

question: For a scalp aplasia cutis congenita lesion that is large, deep, irregular, or membranous, particularly when accompanied by a hair collar sign and/or midline vertex location, what evaluation step is indicated and why?
answer: Imaging studies are indicated to assess for underlying abnormalities such as bone defects, vascular anomalies, or brain malformations. This is because such lesion characteristics (large, deep, irregular, membranous, with hair collar or midline vertex location) raise concern for deeper structural involvement beyond the skin. [Chapter: 64 Developmental Anomalies, p.1306]

question: In fractional photothermolysis, what are microscopic treatment zones (MTZs), and why does the surrounding unaffected skin matter for healing?
answer: MTZs are precisely calibrated columns or cylinders of epidermal and dermal thermal (coagulative or ablative) injury delivered in controlled, defined depth, width, and density with each scan or stamp of a fractional device, rather than treating the entire spot size as with traditional lasers. Each MTZ is surrounded by normal, unaffected skin that acts as a reservoir for healing, allowing these micro-wounds to resolve quickly and with minimal discomfort; histologically they appear as microscopic epidermal necrotic debris (MENDs), which are extruded as the skin surface heals within about 7 days. [Chapter: 137 Lasers and Other Energy-Based Therapies, p.2877-2878]

question: What is the characteristic anatomic location for fluoroscopy-induced radiation dermatitis in patients who have undergone cardiac catheterization procedures, and what late clinical changes may develop at this site as the injury evolves over time?
answer: The left upper back is the characteristic location for fluoroscopy-induced radiation dermatitis in patients with cardiovascular disease who have undergone cardiac catheterizations with attempts at revascularization (e.g., angioplasty, stent placement). Although the injury may initially be acute, over time it can evolve to show epilation of hair, desquamation, telangiectasias, permanent erythema, and eventually ulceration due to dermal necrosis. Severe cases can extend beyond the skin into the subcutaneous fat and muscle. [Chapter: 88 Environmental and Sports-Related Skin Diseases, p.1920]

question: According to this excerpt, what percentage of patients with clinically node-negative cutaneous melanoma greater than 1 mm in depth are found to have microscopic lymph node involvement on sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB), and what histologic features of the primary melanoma are associated with increased rates of SLNB positivity?
answer: Approximately 15%–20% of patients with clinically node-negative cutaneous melanoma greater than 1 mm in depth will have microscopic lymph node involvement detected on SLNB. Increased rates of SLNB positivity are associated with greater tumor thickness and other adverse histologic features of the primary melanoma, including ulceration, high mitotic index, and lymphovascular invasion. [Chapter: 113 Melanoma, p.2451-2452]

question: According to the PUVA treatment schedule, how should the UVA dose be adjusted during the clearing phase if a patient develops painful erythema with or without edema or blistering, and how does this differ from the response to minimal (asymptomatic) erythema?
answer: If a patient develops painful erythema (with or without edema or blistering), treatment should be withheld until symptoms subside, and then the last dose should be reduced by 50%, with further increases limited to 10% increments thereafter. In contrast, if a patient develops only minimal or persistent asymptomatic erythema, treatment is resumed after symptoms resolve and the UVA dose can be increased by 30%. This reflects a more cautious approach when erythema is painful or accompanied by blistering, compared to mild asymptomatic erythema. [Chapter: 134 Ultraviolet Therapy, p.2843-2844]

question: Incontinentia pigmenti (IP) is usually antenatally lethal in boys, yet occasional boys are born with clinically typical IP. According to the excerpt, what two mechanisms explain the occurrence of IP in males, and what is the underlying genetic cause of IP in general?
answer: IP is caused by mutations in IKBKG (NEMO) located at Xq28, with about 80% of patients having a common large deletion of exons 4–10 that typically arises during paternal meiosis. Clinically typical IP in boys can occur due to Klinefelter syndrome (in about 10% of male patients, providing an extra X chromosome) or due to genomic mosaicism from a half-chromatid or postzygotic NEMO mutation, in which case skin lesion distribution may be relatively limited. [Chapter: 62 Mosaicism and Linear Lesions, p.1241-1242]

question: How do elevated atypical papular target lesions (seen in EM) differ from flat atypical target lesions (seen in SJS/TEN), and what accounts for the difference?
answer: Both types of atypical target lesions are round, EM-like lesions with only two zones and/or a poorly defined border. However, the atypical papular lesions of EM are edematous and palpable, whereas the atypical macular lesions of SJS/TEN are flat and non-palpable, except for a possible central vesicle or bulla. This distinction in palpability is what separates the two entities. [Chapter: 20 Erythema Multiforme, Stevens–Johnson Syndrome, and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis, p.436]
chapter: 20 Erythema Multiforme, Stevens–Johnson Syndrome, and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis

question: Why might delaying full-thickness skin graft (FTSG) placement for 7–14 days be beneficial when reconstructing deep nasal tip or alar defects with exposed cartilage, particularly in smokers or patients with prior radiotherapy?
answer: Delaying graft placement allows granulation tissue to fill in the defect, which can achieve a better contour, and the early granulating wound provides an excellent vascular bed. This is especially useful in patients with reduced wound bed vascularity, such as smokers or those with prior radiotherapy, as it increases the likelihood of graft survival. [Chapter: 148 Grafts, p.3054]

question: Why is direct immunofluorescence (DIF) considered the most reliable diagnostic test for pemphigus, and what should be suspected if the DIF result is negative?
answer: DIF directly demonstrates in vivo bound IgG deposition on keratinocyte cell surfaces in perilesional skin or mucous membrane, and IgG deposition is found in up to 100% of patients with active pemphigus vulgaris and pemphigus foliaceus, making it the most reliable and sensitive diagnostic test for all forms of pemphigus. If the DIF is negative, the diagnosis of pemphigus should be seriously questioned. [Chapter: 29 Pemphigus, p.647]

question: Regarding localized lichen myxedematosus occurring in HIV-infected patients, what clinical forms were most commonly seen, what laboratory abnormality was frequently present, and was visceral mucin deposition observed?
answer: In HIV-infected patients, localized lichen myxedematosus most often presented as either the discrete papular form or the nodular variant, with lesions on the limbs and trunk, and HIV infection preceded onset of the mucinosis in all cases. Most patients had hypergammaglobulinemia (a recognized HIV manifestation), while only two had paraproteinemia; the significance of the association with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), seen in up to 10% of HIV-infected individuals, remains unclear. None of the patients had visceral involvement due to mucin deposition. [Chapter: 46 Mucinoses, p.940-941]

question: What is the proposed mechanism behind retinoid-induced nyctalopia, and which retinoid has been associated with osteoporosis but not acitretin or isotretinoin?
answer: Nyctalopia (reduced night vision) is thought to result from competitive inhibition of ocular retinol dehydrogenase by retinoids, which leads to decreased rhodopsin formation. Osteoporosis has been observed with hypervitaminosis A and after long-term therapy with etretinate, but not with acitretin or isotretinoin. [Chapter: 126 Retinoids, p.2702]

question: What clinical and trichoscopic findings characterize folliculitis decalvans, and what is the most effective antibiotic regimen for achieving the longest remission?
answer: Folliculitis decalvans typically affects young to middle-aged men, predominantly on the vertex and occipital scalp, with recurrent follicular pustules, perifollicular erythema, scaling, erosions, and hemorrhagic crusts in the active phase. Its hallmark is hair tufts (5–20+ hairs per follicular unit), which on trichoscopy appear as tufted hairs with perifollicular hyperplasia in a starburst pattern; active inflammation is often seen at the margins of alopecic patches. A 10-week course of clindamycin plus rifampin produced the longest remission compared to doxycycline or azithromycin, which had shorter remission times. [Chapter: 69 Alopecias, p.1436]

question: In systemic mastocytosis (SM), how is the diagnosis of indolent SM, smoldering SM, aggressive SM, and mast cell leukemia (MCL) distinguished based on the presence of B and C findings and bone marrow mast cell percentage?
answer: Indolent SM is diagnosed when there are fewer than 2 B findings and no C findings. Smoldering SM is diagnosed when there are 2 or more B findings but no C findings. When at least 1 C finding is present (with or without B findings), the diagnosis is either aggressive SM, if bone marrow smears show less than 20% mast cells, or MC leukemia, if bone marrow smears show 20% or more mast cells. [Chapter: 118 Mastocytosis, p.2574-2575]

question: According to the excerpt, why does lipoatrophy from insulin injections tend to be prevented by rotating injection sites, and why is it now fairly rare with certain modern insulin therapies?
answer: Repeated use of the same injection site increases the risk of lipoatrophy, so regularly rotating injection sites largely prevents it. Lipoatrophy is also fairly rare with the use of human insulin (as opposed to non-human insulin) and with insulin pump therapy, likely reflecting reduced immunogenicity and less repetitive trauma to a single site. [Chapter: 101 Lipodystrophies, p.2142-2143]

question: According to the key features for phlebology and treatment of leg veins, what general principles should guide the order and technique of treating the superficial venous system with sclerosing agents?
answer: All affected portions of the superficial venous system should ideally be treated in one session, beginning with the most proximal veins, and larger veins should be treated before smaller ones, proceeding from proximal to distal. Additionally, sclerosing agents should be used at the minimal concentration and volume needed to achieve the desired effect while still producing permanent fibrosis of the entire vascular wall. [Chapter: 155 Phlebology and Treatment of Leg Veins, p.3156]
chapter: 155 Phlebology and Treatment of Leg Veins

question: According to the stepwise classification approach for CTCL described in this excerpt, what percentage of CTCL cases are correctly classified after step two, and what does step two specifically require in the evaluation of skin biopsies?
answer: After the first two steps of the classification approach, approximately 90% of CTCL cases will be classified correctly. Step two specifically requires that evaluation of skin biopsies from patients with (suspected) CTCL always include CD30 immunostaining, since this step focuses on identifying the primary cutaneous CD30-positive lymphoproliferative disorders, including cutaneous ALCL (C-ALCL) and lymphomatoid papulosis (LyP). [Chapter: 120 Cutaneous T Cell Lymphoma, p.2605]

question: How can CHILD syndrome be clinically differentiated from Conradi–Hünermann–Happle syndrome, given that both may present with ichthyosiform skin changes along the lines of Blaschko and skeletal abnormalities?
answer: In Conradi–Hünermann–Happle syndrome, the ichthyosiform erythroderma is not unilateral (unlike the unilateral erythema of CHILD syndrome) and resolves into atrophoderma by 2 years of age, whereas CHILD syndrome skin lesions remain unilateral and progress to verrucous hyperkeratosis. Additionally, the skeletal defects in Conradi–Hünermann–Happle syndrome are usually less severe than the ipsilateral skeletal hemidysplasia seen in CHILD syndrome. [Chapter: 57 Ichthyoses, Erythrokeratodermas, and Related Disorders, p.1128]

question: During a longitudinal (lateral) nail biopsy procedure, what complication can result from leaving residual lateral nail matrix tissue, and what is a key technical error to avoid when detaching the matrix from the underlying bone?
answer: Residual lateral nail matrix tissue left behind can lead to nail spicule formation. When detaching the matrix from the bone at the proximal tip of the specimen, care must be taken not to curve the scissors upward too soon, as this foreshortens the specimen and risks leaving matrix tissue behind. [Chapter: 149 Nail Surgery, p.3070]

question: Regarding pediatric burn injuries in the US, what proportion may be attributable to abuse or neglect, and what is the male to female ratio for burns in children?
answer: Abuse or neglect may account for up to 20% of pediatric burns, and the male to female ratio for burns in children is approximately 2:1. [Chapter: 88 Environmental and Sports-Related Skin Diseases, p.1916]

question: According to this excerpt, what are the key clinical and molecular features of Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), including its inheritance pattern, incidence, characteristic skin findings, and the function of its protein product?
answer: NF1 is an autosomal dominant disorder occurring in about 1 in 2000–3000 births, with up to 50% of cases arising from new spontaneous mutations rather than inheritance. Characteristic clinical features include café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, axillary/groin freckling, Lisch nodules, bony defects, and nevus anemicus. Patients also have increased risk for juvenile xanthogranulomas, juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia, and extracutaneous tumors such as optic pathway gliomas, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors, and pheochromocytomas. The NF1 gene product, neurofibromin, functions in the negative regulation of RAS signaling. [Chapter: 61 Neurofibromatosis and Tuberous Sclerosis Complex, p.1210-1211]

question: Why is the retroauricular flap considered one of the best vascularized random pattern tissue importation flaps, and what advantage does this confer for defects such as those of the helical rim, antihelix, and scapha?
answer: Although the retroauricular flap is a random pattern flap without a single dedicated vascular pedicle, it derives a rich blood supply from the scalp skin, making it one of the best vascularized random pattern tissue importation flaps. This robust vascularity allows it to easily support cartilage grafts when needed, making it especially useful for repairing large defects of the helical rim, antihelix, and scapha. [Chapter: 147 Flaps, p.3040-3041]

question: What is the significance of identifying mycobacterial DNA sequences and the mKatG catalase-peroxidase protein from Mycobacterium tuberculosis in the study of sarcoidosis, and what other evidence supports an infectious etiology?
answer: These findings support the hypothesis that sarcoidosis may have an infectious trigger, with mKatG proposed as a potential antigen driving granulomatous inflammation. A meta-analysis found mycobacterial nucleic acids in approximately 25% of sarcoidal tissues. Additional supporting evidence for an infectious cause includes the transmissibility of sarcoidal lesions via the Kveim reagent and the development of sarcoidal granulomas in organ transplant recipients who received organs from donors with sarcoidosis. [Chapter: 93 Non-infectious Granulomas, p.2002-2003]

question: According to the color chart in the basic principles chapter, what mechanisms or diseases can produce black-colored skin lesions?
answer: Black skin lesions can result from necrosis due to vasculopathy (e.g., levamisole-contaminated cocaine), vasculitis (e.g., granulomatosis with polyangiitis), thrombosis (e.g., DIC, monoclonal cryoglobulinemia), emboli (e.g., ecthyma gangrenosum), vasospasm (e.g., severe Raynaud phenomenon), or vascular compromise (e.g., atherosclerosis, calciphylaxis). Black color can also occur with eschar formation (e.g., anthrax), cutaneous melanoma, or traumatic tattoo (e.g., asphalt). [Chapter: 0 Basic Principles of Dermatology, p.36-37]

question: According to this excerpt, what historical observations did Pliny the Younger and Ramazzini each make regarding occupationally induced skin disease?
answer: Pliny the Younger, writing in the first century CE, recorded dermatitis in individuals after they cut down pine trees, which likely represented allergic contact dermatitis to colophony in pine resin. Ramazzini, in his 1700 treatise, described irritant contact dermatitis of the hands and forearms occurring in soap and laundry workers. [Chapter: 16 Occupational Dermatoses, p.368-369]

question: According to the excerpt, what percentage of chronic urticaria cases are spontaneous versus inducible, and what are the four subcategories (with approximate percentages) that make up spontaneous chronic urticaria?
answer: Chronic urticaria is 75% spontaneous (non-physical, non-vasculitic) and 25% inducible. Within the spontaneous category, the subtypes are approximately 45% idiopathic, 25% autoimmune, 20% pseudoallergic, and 5% infection-related (with the remaining 5% likely representing another category). [Chapter: 18 Urticaria and Angioedema, p.405-406]

question: According to the 1997 update of the 1982 ACR revised classification criteria for SLE, what three findings can satisfy the 'immunologic disorder' criterion?
answer: The immunologic disorder criterion can be met by any of the following: (a) an abnormal titer of anti-DNA antibody to native DNA; (b) presence of anti-Sm antibody (antibody to Sm nuclear antigen); or (c) a positive finding of antiphospholipid antibodies, which includes an abnormal IgG or IgM anticardiolipin antibody level, a positive lupus anticoagulant test, or a false-positive syphilis serology persisting for at least 6 months and confirmed by FTA-ABS or TPI testing. [Chapter: 41 Lupus Erythematosus, p.858-859]

question: According to this excerpt on managing Darier disease, why are oral retinoids generally reserved for patients with severe disease unresponsive to topical treatment, and in which clinical presentation should they be avoided?
answer: Systemic retinoids (isotretinoin, acitretin, alitretinoin) are highly effective, improving ~90% of patients, but their use is limited by side effects such as mucocutaneous dryness and elevated serum lipids, relapse after stopping therapy, and teratogenicity requiring mandatory contraception in women of childbearing potential—so they are reserved for severe, topical-treatment-refractory cases. They are not recommended in patients with predominantly bullous or intertriginous lesions, as oral retinoids may actually aggravate the disease in this presentation. [Chapter: 59 Darier Disease and Hailey–Hailey Disease, p.1171]

question: According to this excerpt, what are the absolute contraindications to cyclosporine use, and what caution should be exercised regarding drug interactions?
answer: Absolute contraindications to cyclosporine include significant renal impairment, uncontrolled hypertension, and hypersensitivity to cyclosporine. Regarding drug interactions, drugs that inhibit the CYP3A4 pathway will increase cyclosporine levels, while CYP3A4 inducers will decrease its effectiveness by lowering serum levels; additionally, drugs such as NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, vancomycin, and trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole can potentiate renal toxicity when combined with cyclosporine. [Chapter: 130 Other Systemic Drugs, p.2787]

question: Why is the lateral cheek along the zygomatic prominence considered a less risky area for filler injection compared to the superior nasolabial fold or medial cheek, and what injection technique is appropriate there?
answer: The lateral cheek is considered less risky because, although the zygomaticofacial artery sits on the periosteum there, this is a more predictable vascular depth compared to the superior nasolabial fold (where the angular artery becomes subcutaneous) or the medial cheek (where the infraorbital artery runs periosteally and the angular artery subcutaneously). Because of this, injection along the periosteum with either a needle or cannula is considered appropriate in the lateral cheek. [Chapter: 158 Injectable Soft Tissue Augmentation, p.3202-3203]

question: According to the excerpt, at what concentration and vehicle is Methylisothiazolinone tested in the relevant screening series?
answer: Methylisothiazolinone is tested at a concentration of 0.2% in an aqueous vehicle (0.2% aq). [Chapter: 14 Allergic Contact Dermatitis, p.332-333]

question: According to epidemiologic studies of childhood-onset atopic dermatitis (AD), what proportion of affected individuals develop the disease by 6 months, by 1 year, and by 5 years of age, and what percentage go into remission by age 12?
answer: Childhood-onset AD, the most common type, develops during the first 6 months of life in 45% of affected individuals, during the first year of life in 60%, and before 5 years of age in 85%. About 60% of infants and young children with AD go into remission by 12 years of age, including a subset who resolve by 4–6 years of age, while in others disease activity persists into adolescence and adulthood. [Chapter: 12 Atopic Dermatitis, p.281-282]

question: For blocking the infraorbital nerve, why is the intraoral approach preferred over the percutaneous approach, and how is it performed?
answer: The intraoral approach is preferred because it is less painful and more reliable than the percutaneous technique. The needle is inserted between the first and second premolars (bicuspids) and advanced cephalad parallel to the periosteum until the horizontal portion of the maxillary bone is reached, then pulled back slightly before injecting the anesthetic. Applying a topical anesthetic to the mucosa a couple of minutes before injection can further reduce the pain of needle insertion. [Chapter: 143 Anesthesia, p.2969-2970]

question: How does the age distribution of precursor B lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia differ from other cutaneous B cell lymphomas, and how should even apparently skin-limited cases be managed?
answer: Unlike other cutaneous B cell lymphomas, precursor B lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia shows a clear predilection for children and young adults. Patients typically present with solitary large erythematous tumors on the head and neck, and elevated serum LDH reflects its aggressive, often systemic nature. Because of this aggressiveness, all patients—even those without documented systemic involvement at presentation—should be assumed to have, and treated for, systemic disease. [Chapter: 119 B Cell Lymphomas of the Skin, p.2585-2586]
chapter: 119 B Cell Lymphomas of the Skin

question: How is an open use test performed, and what is the purpose of a repeat open application test?
answer: In an open use test (the "poor man's patch test"), the patient applies the suspected product twice daily for 1–2 weeks to a predetermined, non-dermatitic site such as the antecubital fossa or flexor forearm; if dermatitis develops, the patient is considered to be reacting to that product, though this method cannot identify the specific causative ingredient. Repeat open application tests serve a related but distinct purpose: they help establish the clinical relevance of a positive patch test result, for example confirming whether a low concentration of an allergen (like fragrance) that did not react on initial patch testing is still clinically significant when used in an actual product. [Chapter: 14 Allergic Contact Dermatitis, p.335-336]

question: In immunocompetent individuals with latent HSV-1 infection, recurrent herpes labialis most commonly appears at which site, and what other, less common sites can be affected?
answer: Recurrent HSV-1 lesions most often appear on the vermilion border of the lip. Less commonly, they can occur on perioral skin, nasal mucosa, the cheek, and attached oral mucosa overlying bone, such as the gingiva and hard palate. [Chapter: 80 Human Herpesviruses, p.1712]

question: In a Canadian trial of incompletely excised BCC, how did adjuvant radiotherapy affect the 5-year and 10-year local control rates compared to no adjuvant radiotherapy, and why were the 10-year rates similar between groups?
answer: Adjuvant radiotherapy improved the 5-year local control rate from 61% to 91% compared with no adjuvant treatment. However, by 10 years the local control rates were similar between groups (92% vs 90%), because most recurrences in the non-radiotherapy group were successfully salvaged with surgery. [Chapter: 139 Radiotherapy, p.2911-2912]

question: What causes carpet beetle dermatitis, what is the typical clinical presentation, and how is it managed?
answer: Carpet beetle dermatitis is a hypersensitivity reaction to the hastae (larval hairs) or hemolymph of Dermestidae beetles (Attagenus, Dermestes, Anthrenus, Trogaderma spp.), whose larvae feed on household organic materials like wool and hide in rugs and furniture.
